learningObjectives.title: Production, productivity and division of labour
The role of money and financial markets

questions.q: According to the law of demand, what normally happens to the quantity demanded of a good when its price rises, all else being equal?
options: Quantity demanded rises
Quantity demanded falls
Quantity demanded stays exactly the same
Quantity supplied falls
questions.explain: The law of demand states that, ceteris paribus, a rise in price leads to a fall in the quantity demanded.

questions.q: Which of the following would cause the demand curve for tea to shift to the right?
options: A fall in the price of tea itself
A rise in the price of tea itself
A rise in the price of coffee, a substitute
An increase in the number of tea producers
questions.explain: A higher price of a substitute (coffee) increases demand for tea, shifting its demand curve rightwards.

questions.q: A change in the price of a good itself causes which of the following?
options: A shift of the demand curve
A movement along the demand curve
A shift of both demand and supply curves
No change at all
questions.explain: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the curve (an extension or contraction), not a shift.

questions.q: What is the correct formula for price elasticity of demand (PED)?
options: % change in price / % change in quantity demanded
% change in quantity demanded / % change in price
% change in quantity demanded / % change in income
% change in quantity supplied / % change in price
questions.explain: PED is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.

questions.q: A good has a price elasticity of demand with a value greater than 1 (ignoring the sign). This means demand is:
options: Price inelastic
Perfectly inelastic
Price elastic
Of unitary elasticity
questions.explain: A PED greater than 1 means quantity demanded is relatively responsive to price, so demand is price elastic.

questions.q: When the price of a product rises by 10%, the quantity demanded falls by 20%. What is the price elasticity of demand?
questions.explain: PED = -20% / 10% = -2, indicating price-elastic demand.

questions.q: What does price elasticity of supply (PES) measure?
options: The responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in price
The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price
The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in income
The total revenue earned by producers
questions.explain: PES measures how much the quantity supplied changes in response to a change in price.

questions.q: In a market, the equilibrium price is best described as the price at which:
options: Supply is greater than demand
Demand is greater than supply
Quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
Producers make the largest possible profit
questions.explain: Equilibrium occurs where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, so there is no tendency for price to change.

questions.q: If the current market price of a good is set above the equilibrium price, what is the most likely outcome?
options: Excess demand, pushing the price up
Excess supply, pushing the price down
A permanent shortage of the good
The demand curve shifts left
questions.explain: A price above equilibrium creates excess supply (a surplus), which puts downward pressure on price.

questions.q: Which of the following is a typical benefit of greater competition between firms for consumers?
options: Higher prices
Lower prices and improved quality
Reduced choice of products
Fewer new products entering the market
questions.explain: Competition encourages firms to lower prices, raise quality and innovate to attract consumers.

questions.q: The demand for labour is described as a 'derived demand' because it:
options: Depends on the wage rate alone
Is derived from the demand for the goods and services labour produces
Always falls as wages rise
Is set entirely by the government
questions.explain: Firms demand labour to produce goods and services, so labour demand is derived from demand for output.

questions.q: In a competitive labour market, the number of skilled software developers falls sharply while firms' demand for them stays the same. What is the likely effect on their wages?
options: Wages rise
Wages fall
Wages stay exactly the same
Wages become zero
questions.explain: A fall in the supply of labour with unchanged demand raises the equilibrium wage.

questions.q: Which economist is famously associated with the concept of the division of labour, illustrated by the example of a pin factory?
options: John Maynard Keynes
Adam Smith
David Ricardo
Milton Friedman
questions.explain: Adam Smith described the division of labour using the pin factory example in 'The Wealth of Nations'.

questions.q: Labour productivity is best defined as:
options: The total number of workers a firm employs
Output produced per worker (or per unit of input)
The total revenue a firm earns
The wage paid to each worker
questions.explain: Productivity measures output per unit of input, such as output per worker.

questions.q: Which of the following is a key advantage of the division of labour and specialisation?
options: Workers become less skilled over time
Increased productivity as workers become skilled at specific tasks
Higher costs per unit of output
A reduction in total output
questions.explain: Specialising in specific tasks raises workers' skill and speed, increasing overall productivity.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the recognised functions of money?
options: A barrier to trade
A medium of exchange
A form of derived demand
A type of elasticity
questions.explain: Money functions as a medium of exchange, a store of value, a unit of account and a standard of deferred payment.

questions.q: When money acts as a 'store of value', this means it:
options: Can be used to compare the value of different goods
Allows purchasing power to be saved and used in the future
Is accepted as payment for goods and services now
Records the amount owed on a loan
questions.explain: As a store of value, money holds its worth over time so it can be saved and spent later.

questions.q: What is a key role of financial markets and banks in an economy?
options: To set the price of every good
To channel funds from savers to borrowers
To abolish the use of money
To fix wages in the labour market
questions.explain: Financial markets and banks act as intermediaries, transferring savings to those who wish to borrow and invest.

questions.q: A shop displays a jumper priced at 25 pounds so customers can compare it with other items. Which function of money is being used here?
options: Store of value
Medium of exchange
Unit of account
Standard of deferred payment
questions.explain: Displaying a price to measure and compare value is money acting as a unit of account.

questions.q: A market dominated by a single seller with no close competitors is known as a:
options: Monopoly
Perfect competition
Free market
Labour market
questions.explain: A monopoly exists when a single firm dominates the market with no close competitors.
